items.postText:
Saturday morning, I made the mistake of telling Artemis we would go out after I checked one thing. She looked toward the door and accepted this as an actual commitment. I appreciated her optimism until she began organizing her morning around it. My coffee was still hot enough to support the plan. Fat Cat occupied the couch with his paws folded and his expectations already settled. I opened the material about health insurance denials and tried to locate the part where the arrangement became reasonable. A doctor examines a patient and recommends treatment. An insurance company can then decide the treatment lacks medical necessity. I wanted to know who made that second judgment and what they actually knew about the person. That seemed like a question I could investigate before finishing breakfast. Some of you heard “a quick look” and started making plans. I cannot be responsible for the optimism you brought into this. Artemis had made the same mistake and at least had the excuse of being a dog.

The closet made a noise before I had finished explaining the problem aloud. Artemis lifted her head and watched the door. The Soapbox slid out with a small notice attached to its front. Someone had printed NOT AN OBSTRUCTION in letters large enough to read from the hallway it was partially occupying. I examined the notice while Artemis examined the available space. She stepped over the box and continued toward the door. I read the notice twice. The second reading did very little for the doorway. Fat Cat watched me consider the relationship between the wording and the wood. His expression suggested that my investigation was already running behind the dog’s. I picked the damn thing up and moved it. The notice remained perfectly legible. Then I climbed onto it and became a taller part of the problem.

I have worked in healthcare and healthcare-adjacent roles long enough to resent how easily somebody else’s administrative decision becomes the patient’s additional responsibility. The patient gets another call to make. Their clinician gets another demand for documentation. Somewhere in this arrangement, the organization collecting money for coverage gets to explain why everybody else needs to do more work. My irritation concerns a particularly consequential judgment: the insurer deciding that recommended treatment is medically unnecessary. That conclusion reaches straight into the patient’s available choices. A person who cannot afford the treatment without coverage has very little use for a lecture about the difference between denying payment and denying care. They still need the money before they can obtain the treatment. Calling the decision administrative leaves that problem sitting exactly where it was. This is why the question of practicing medicine without a license keeps coming up. Somebody is exercising power over a medical decision while insisting that we appreciate the precise wording of their involvement. I appreciate that the patient is still waiting. The well-paid bastards responsible for that decision owe the patient something more useful than a vocabulary lesson.

My first reaction was to demand that the person overruling the doctor actually examine the patient. Then my own medical history interrupted me. As I have previously described, a physician familiar with my wrist injury later handled documentation without requiring another appointment. He already knew the relevant problem. Another waiting room would have added travel and another opportunity for me to complain about parking. His knowledge of my circumstances was what made the judgment useful. That brings me directly to the reviewer’s work. What records did they consider before rejecting the treating clinician’s recommendation? Their relevant expertise belongs beside the reasoning. A signature can identify a doctor without establishing that the doctor adequately investigated the decision. Putting physician review on the notice leaves the actual reviewing to be done. We have somehow arrived at the luxurious premium feature where the reviewer knows what the hell they are reviewing.

William George Eskew had lung cancer and was being treated at MD Anderson. On February 3, 2016, his doctor submitted an urgent request for proton radiation therapy. The request described the risk that radiation could damage organs near the treatment area. His esophagus was among the structures the doctor wanted to protect. Sierra Health and Life denied coverage two days later. Its denial relied on a UnitedHealthcare policy classifying proton therapy for lung cancer as unproven and not medically necessary. The treatment request, denial, and policy exhibits put the warning and the response in the record. The policy also directed reviewers to consult the member’s particular coverage document. That document controlled when its terms conflicted with the general policy. I kept those instructions in mind while reading what the reviewer said he had done. There was a patient with a particular risk and a contract governing his coverage. Both required attention before the company could credibly claim that its general answer settled his request.

The reviewing physician was Shamoon Ahmad, a medical oncologist. In his trial testimony, he acknowledged his lack of training in radiation oncology. He testified that he reviewed records. He also acknowledged that he did not contact treating oncologist Zhongxing Liao about the request. Eskew’s particular insurance contract went unread by him as well. Ahmad described familiarity with standard contract terms and reliance on nurses to identify differences. So the patient received a denial from a physician who had skipped the contract the policy told him to consult. The treating oncologist had identified an organ-damage risk that deserved an individualized answer. Employing a doctor did nothing to make those omitted steps happen. Selling coverage while treating its actual terms as optional reading is some breathtakingly arrogant shit. The policy had already told him where to look. God forbid the paid expert follow the company’s own fucking instructions.

Eskew received a different form of radiation treatment after the denial. His esophagus was damaged and he endured severe suffering during the remainder of his life. The jury awarded forty million dollars in compensatory damages and another hundred sixty million in punitive damages. On August 5, 2024, the Nevada Supreme Court affirmed the judgment against Sierra. The appellate majority found substantial evidence supporting insurance bad faith. Its account described the company’s reliance on the general policy without a thorough investigation of Eskew’s specific needs. Sierra challenged the judgment, and two justices disagreed with the majority over damages and trial issues. The award survived that appeal. The jury instructions excluded any claim that Sierra caused or contributed to his death. His treating physician also had not pursued an appeal before selecting the alternative treatment, a decision I will return to. The finding of bad faith and the injury established in this case already give us plenty to confront. Eskew had needed a decision that properly addressed his circumstances while it could still protect him. A judgment years later could establish responsibility for what happened. It could never give him those years back without the suffering. I put the coffee down and continued reading.

The federal inspector general found problems extending beyond one patient’s litigation. Its 2022 Medicare Advantage investigation examined a sample of denials from fifteen large organizations during one week in June 2019. Investigators estimated that thirteen percent of denied prior-authorization requests met Medicare coverage rules. Some requests had been rejected for insufficient documentation even though the existing medical records supported necessity. The information was already there. Somebody had supplied what the review needed and still received a denial citing insufficient information. Perhaps they could resubmit it with a polite arrow pointing toward the part somebody missed. I doubt the premium comes with a discount for helping the insurer locate material already in its possession. The resulting work falls on somebody trying to obtain care and somebody trying to provide it. The report now lists its recommendations as implemented. Those changes came after requests meeting the coverage rules had been denied. The people affected had already been handed a problem the records should have prevented.

A doctor’s involvement can also become remarkably difficult to reconcile with the speed of the alleged work. The March 2025 order in the Cigna PxDx litigation describes allegations involving more than three hundred thousand payment requests over two months in 2022. The alleged average review time was 1.2 seconds per request. These were payment claims, including care already received. The court allowed certain claims to proceed at the pleading stage. Cigna disputed the challenge to its medical-director review process. An average like that makes meaningful individual consideration sound awfully fucking ambitious. A clinician’s name attached to a decision gives the customer someone to imagine doing the work. When I read physician review, I picture somebody considering what the patient’s record says. Apparently I have been bringing an extravagant set of expectations to the word review. Try including the alleged average in the sales brochure and see whether marketing still wants it in readable print. I suspect the font discussion would receive substantially more individual attention.

Even a reviewer who reads the file can work under instructions that make independent judgment an awkward career choice. In November 2023, STAT reported that naviHealth managers wanted rehabilitation stays kept within one percent of the days projected by an algorithm. Former employees described exposure to discipline when they missed the target. UnitedHealth’s response described the tool as a guide for planning and said coverage decisions followed Medicare criteria and plan terms. That description has to contend with the reported consequences for employees who departed from the projections. A human reviewer needs the authority to conclude that the patient requires more time. Their patient may recover more slowly than the estimate. The clinical reason for extending care has to count for something when management evaluates the employee. On the reported arrangement, disagreeing with the tool could create a performance problem for the person doing the reviewing. I would love to hear that explained during recruitment for a job requiring independent medical judgment. The applicant could save everybody some time by asking which answer management prefers before bothering with the patient. A human signature offers little comfort when the employee must worry about being punished for exercising the judgment advertised to the public. Calling the software helpful does fuck all to answer who can overrule it.

The financial calculations deserve the same attention as the medical ones. The Senate’s October 2024 majority-staff report on post-acute care described UnitedHealthcare’s post-acute denial rate rising from 10.9 percent in 2020 to 22.7 percent in 2022. It also examined CVS calculations involving hundreds of millions of dollars in avoided inpatient-facility medical costs. Those are organizational records about decisions with financial consequences. A spreadsheet can record the smaller bill while leaving the patient’s condition entirely unexplained. The patients’ outcomes belong in the same assessment as the costs. An executive claiming efficiency should be able to discuss what happened to the people involved. Otherwise I can produce an impressive household savings report by announcing that Artemis will receive less food. She will immediately supply the missing outcome assessment. Fat Cat opened one eye when my voice rose. I told him I was discussing the quality of management. He closed it before I could pretend the subject was unfamiliar. Some of you are giving me the same look, and I already maintain a cat for that purpose. My own supervisor at least makes his dissatisfaction available without requiring an appeal.

Patients experience the delay in those decisions while remaining sick. In a study of ongoing oral anticancer treatment, researchers examined Medicare prescription claims involving eleven oral anticancer drugs. Adding prior authorization was associated with a 9.7-day increase in time until the next prescription fill. The study also found higher odds of treatment discontinuation. These patients had already been receiving the medication. A new administrative requirement had been introduced between them and the next refill. Their illness continued on its own schedule throughout the additional process. Having started cancer treatment apparently failed to establish that continuing it deserved some fucking urgency. Imagine explaining the value of that extra wait at a meeting where everyone already has their medication. The people designing the requirement get to finish the meeting and continue their day. The patient still has to get the prescription filled. The research here documents harm without supplying a national total of deaths caused by insurer denials. Those additional days still have to be lived through by the person waiting for treatment.

Artemis returned to the doorway while I was reading about the additional work required to get an answer. I told her we were nearly finished. She considered the available evidence and lay down. I decided this represented confidence in my leadership because the alternative would have required an apology. The appeal in Eskew’s case brings us back to a clinician deciding what more process would accomplish. Liao acknowledged that she had not pursued an appeal or a peer-to-peer call. She also testified that she had not read the denial letter before selecting the alternative treatment. Her explanation concerned previous unsuccessful appeals and the delays she anticipated. Sierra emphasized the availability of expedited review within seventy-two hours. The testimony records both positions. That appeal was never attempted, so its actual duration remains unknown. What the record does show is a treating clinician who expected the available correction process to consume time she believed the patient needed. An insurer’s published deadline cannot by itself make clinicians trust that process. The organization has to earn that trust through decisions and timely correction. Congratulations on the appeal procedure your patient’s doctor expected to take time he could not spare.

Across Medicare Advantage, most denied requests never reach an appeal. KFF’s analysis of the 2024 data found that only 11.5 percent of denials were appealed. Of those appeals, 80.7 percent were fully or partly overturned. Those figures describe appeal outcomes and cannot independently establish the original error rate. They do show how consequential reconsideration was among the requests that reached it. Obtaining that reconsideration requires someone to act. The patient or someone helping them has to understand the denial and prepare a response. Their clinician may need to defend a recommendation already explained in the original request. A relative can end up fitting the insurer’s additional work around employment and caregiving. The company continues to describe the availability of this activity as a safeguard. I keep looking at who has to perform it. An ill person should not need exceptional persistence and a spare family member to obtain a competent answer about covered care. The industry has managed to make the customer’s determination sound like a feature of the service. Try boasting that your product works especially well for customers healthy enough to argue with you.

Once that additional work fails to prevent harm, the organization’s preferred description of its role becomes especially convenient. Washington’s RCW 48.43.545 addresses carrier liability for certain harmful denials, delays, or modifications of medically necessary care. It expressly bars a carrier from invoking laws against its practicing medicine as a defense in an action under that section. Apparently someone in Olympia anticipated an insurer becoming fascinated by professional boundaries after its decision had affected a patient’s treatment. The statute has conditions concerning substantial harm and independent review, and federal law can affect the claim. Within that framework, the carrier has an obligation it cannot dissolve by pointing at its business description. That brings me back to the question that put me on this box. Whether a particular act violates licensing law depends on the conduct and the applicable law. Eskew’s case establishes bad faith involving a physician reviewer whose credentials did nothing to prevent the inadequate investigation identified by the court. The clinical authority being exercised deserves scrutiny all the way through the decision. An organization cannot earn my trust merely by locating a doctor somewhere between receiving the request and issuing the rejection. The person suffering the consequences needs the work to have been done properly. The company’s preferred wording contributes absolutely nothing to repairing the harm.

The injured patient can then discover that the arrangement behind their coverage affects the remedy available. In Aetna Health v. Davila, the Supreme Court held that ERISA displaced the state claims before it over allegedly harmful benefit denials. Claims falling within that rule proceed through the federal framework. Federal remedies include recovery of benefits and certain other relief. They do not simply reproduce the ordinary state damages available for personal injury. The route depends on the plan and the legal duty involved. So an injured person can spend time learning how their employer arranged coverage before learning what they can recover. That is a spectacular amount of homework to assign somebody who already had a medical problem. I can almost hear the explanation becoming longer as the useful answer gets further away. The patient’s injury remains the same throughout the discussion. Their route to holding the decision-maker responsible can change with the legal structure surrounding it. Anybody selling this arrangement as adequate accountability should try describing the available recovery in the same plain language used to sell the coverage. Put the practical answer where the customer can find it before they need a lawyer to translate their disappointment.

Companies affected by those rules can afford sustained attention to how the rules are written. UnitedHealth Group reported 2.52 million dollars in federal lobbying expenses for the fourth quarter of 2025. That filing covered several issues, including prior authorization. The resource advantage is visible in the arrangement itself. The organization can pay people to represent its interests while its employees continue running the business. A patient challenging a denial may be trying to get through a call during lunch. Apparently, keeping your own interests represented is worth paying people to do promptly. I am sure the customer would enjoy being represented with the same enthusiasm before their afternoon medication. Political access becomes a routine institutional expense while personal advocacy becomes something the sick person must somehow fit in. The company can maintain its representation after one patient has exhausted their time and energy. Its next meeting can proceed without waiting for that patient to recover. The fucking advantage is right there in who can keep showing up.

Money also changes how readily some concerns receive a senior audience. In a randomized experiment involving 191 congressional offices, Joshua Kalla and David Broockman varied whether prospective meeting attendees were identified as campaign donors. Disclosing donor status increased access to senior officials approximately threefold to fourfold. A constituent’s argument could acquire a more attentive audience because somebody knew about the donation. I have heard enough speeches about listening to ordinary people to find that result insulting. By then the raccoon had appeared outside near the dumpster. Artemis noticed him and delivered an immediate objection through the window. I explained that I was discussing the resources required to get somebody’s attention. She increased her contribution before I could finish. The raccoon had stopped chewing. I chose to interpret that as support, and I would appreciate you not examining my methods until after I finish criticizing theirs. He looked away before I could establish how much agreement I intended to claim. Artemis glanced back when I asked her to lower her volume. My own contribution to the noise had apparently become relevant. Outside, the raccoon resumed his meal and ended my consultation without offering a meeting with anybody senior.

Getting a patient’s experience heard publicly requires another kind of access. The clinical record takes time to reconstruct, and its consequences can disappear behind the phrase denied claim. Reporting such as STAT’s gives those decisions names, instructions, and people whose accounts can be examined. In his December 11, 2024 Atlantic essay, Graeme Wood invoked allocating scarce resources while condemning the killing of Brian Thompson and the celebration surrounding it. Take that general rationale back to the failures already in front of us. Sierra’s own policy directed consultation of the contract its reviewer left unread. OIG found requests that already met Medicare’s rules. I can understand a budget and still recognize a denial that failed independent review. The patronizing economics lecture supplies fuck all of the missing clinical investigation. Apply it to the actual decision and show what it explains.

The reaction around Luigi Mangione made the anger impossible to miss after Thompson was killed in December 2024. Highly visible online responses offered sympathy for Mangione or approval of the killing. That reaction deserves examination on its own terms. In Emerson’s December 11–13, 2024 poll, sixty-eight percent of registered voters called the killer’s actions unacceptable. Seventeen percent called them acceptable. Among respondents aged eighteen through twenty-nine, forty-one percent found the actions acceptable and forty percent found them unacceptable. The youngest group was effectively split in that survey. That is an extraordinary public response to the killing of a stranger. A serious examination has to ask how approval became something people were willing to express publicly. Sneering at the audience does very little to investigate the conditions surrounding that response.

Another December 2024 survey from NORC asked about responsibility for Thompson’s killing. Seventy-eight percent assigned a great deal or moderate amount to the person who committed it. Sixty-nine percent assigned that level of responsibility to health-insurance coverage denials. Respondents could assign responsibility to more than one factor. They nevertheless show that many respondents connected the event to the industry’s conduct. My reading is that perceived failure of ordinary remedies helps explain why some people found a story of retaliation emotionally satisfying. A person who believes complaints accomplish nothing may begin treating an act against an institution as a form of recognition. That interpretation says something bleak about confidence in getting help through ordinary channels. Online feedback can then reward increasingly forceful expressions of the sentiment. Research by William Brady and colleagues found that social feedback and network norms could amplify subsequent outrage expression. An approving audience could similarly reinforce increasingly hostile posts. Someone sees anger rewarded and learns what their audience applauds. The public performance can become more extreme while the underlying grievance remains unresolved. People still need treatment after the approving post has collected its responses. I want the people responsible for harmful decisions held accountable through evidence and law. A shooting leaves another family dealing with a death and supplies no functioning appeal for the next patient. Insurers remain answerable for their own decisions throughout this argument.

That means a reviewer with relevant competence actually considering the patient’s circumstances before rejecting the treating clinician’s recommendation. The explanation has to address the clinical findings that made the treatment necessary in the clinician’s judgment. Washington has adopted individual-review and human-oversight requirements within the statute’s coverage scope. Their value depends on what reviewers actually do with the records. Software assistance still leaves a person responsible for the decision and the use of the tool. Management must allow that person to authorize appropriate care when an individual case warrants departure from a general projection. Correction has to happen while it can still help the patient. An urgent appeal requires usable assistance and an answer within a clinically meaningful period. Evaluating the system also means examining requests people abandoned and recording why appealed decisions changed. Claims of efficiency need evidence about clinical accuracy and consequences alongside the spending figures. Responsibility for demonstrated harm must reach the organization whose conduct caused it. These demands follow directly from the failures already discussed. The industry can begin answering them with the patience it routinely requires from people who are sick.

Artemis went to the door again while I was still considering the final paragraph. Apparently we were still going for a walk, despite everything you had insisted on discussing. I stepped down from the Soapbox and picked up my coffee. It had acquired the temperature appropriate to my claims about brevity. Fat Cat watched me take the first sip and appeared to consider the outcome entirely predictable. I told him I had finished the important part. He closed his eyes without requesting a copy. Outside, the raccoon had already left me to my conclusions. I put the cup down and reached for the leash. Artemis got up before I could make another announcement. I followed her toward the door before my record became any worse.

I keep coming back to the warning in Eskew’s treatment request. The risk to his esophagus was identified before the denial. Somebody had already done the work of explaining what needed protection. The company’s answer helped determine which treatment he received. Years later, a jury could put a dollar figure on the harm. The time when a competent decision might have protected him was already gone. I cannot tolerate having that buried beneath another explanation of procedure. The executives collecting money to run these organizations can take responsibility for the work done under their authority. Spare me the corporate sympathy after the point when competent work could have helped. The next patient needs the care they were promised, and the people collecting the money need to do their goddamn jobs.

So, my medical insurance, Aetna, decided that diagnostic blood work is no longer covered 100%. I received no notification. I first called when I got billed for lab work and was told it was covered completely, then I was told there was a copay. It's not billed as a copay; it's billed as a percentage of two different blood tests that add up to $10.  
Now, I am getting billed for a cardiology rehab I never did. 
It's almost like AI is just making up ways to drain my bank account.

I was scheduled to have knee surgery on Tuesday. Last Friday at 3:30 PM I received a call from the Core Institute that my insurance Aetna denied coverage. You would think they would have cleared it with Aetna before proceeding with all the tests and appointments. I spent six weeks getting everything they needed just to be denied coverage. I should have gone to the VA . Now the VA is my only hope. I have been in pain for over a year now unable to walk without a cane . Has anyone had a similar experience?

Aetna SRP BS 🤬
Has anyone else been having issues with Aetna handling SRP claims?

I have a patient who came in earlier this year for their first visit with us. The treatment included a comprehensive exam, FMX, 2 quads of SRP, and 2 sites of Arestin.

Aetna paid for the comprehensive exam and FMX, but denied the Arestin and initially did not pay the SRP.

The interesting part is that Aetna did pay the SRP on the patient’s other side, which was completed at a separate visit a week later.

I’ve continued sending statements. The patient called, and I advised them to contact Aetna regarding the denial. If Aetna determines something is patient responsibility, then obviously we expect the patient to pay it.

Then Aetna called me yesterday and said the patient was only responsible for the Arestin. I provided the NEA numbers and all the information they needed to reprocess the claim (length of appt, x-rays, perio chart, anesthetic…. you know, how many 2x2’s were used, if we used cotton rolls, what kind of handpieces we use, if we used a saliva ejector… literally all of the stupid questions they ask now 😆)

Today, another Aetna representative called and told me the same thing—that the patient was only responsible for the Arestin. This representative also had no record of yesterday’s call and couldn’t see the previous conversation in the notes.

So I asked:

“If the patient is only responsible for the Arestin, when do you plan on paying for the SRP?”

Because at this point, the patient is being told they don’t owe the balance, while Aetna isn’t paying the provider for a procedure they have already demonstrated they will cover.

I’ve provided the documentation, NEA numbers, and everything else needed to get this reprocessed. The patient is now potentially heading toward collections for a balance that Aetna is essentially saying they shouldn’t owe and they are trying to force a write off. 

The representative was then rushing to get me off the phone.

Has anyone else experienced this with Aetna? Specifically, Aetna paying one side of an SRP case but refusing to pay the other side and then expecting the provider to write off the difference?

How are you handling these situations?

I am very grateful I have insurance.
Im also grateful I involved medicare and had insurance denials of claims reversed...and they are going to be paid.

 But a nurse I know asked "why do we feel like celebrating when we win an appeal for a service that we Knew was covered, but was denied until Medicare got involved"?

I truly believe they deny covered services in hope that we dont appeal and they don't have to pay.

If they deny 1,000 valid claims and 500 dont appeal? How much are money they cheating people out of?

I saw this with my mom, from the VA to geisinger gold, to medicare. If you have no one to advocate for you and you don't understand what to do? You're pretty much screwed.

I recommend finding a person designated to act on our behalf...informing our insurance company who that person is and ensuring they have full access to act on our behalf...

When an insurer denies a treatment, a doctor recommended it and a company overruled the doctor.

That's the whole transaction. One side went to medical school and examined the patient. The other side read a claim code and a cost.

The denial letter never says who made the call. It says "not medically necessary," which is a medical opinion issued by a billing department.

I'm not claiming every claim should be paid. Some shouldn't. I'm saying the person who says no should be as accountable as the person who said yes — and right now one of them has a name and a license, and the other has a letterhead.

A no that costs the insurer nothing isn't a medical decision. It's a pricing decision with a medical vocabulary.

items.postText:
Insurers denied nearly 1 in 5 in-network claims last year.
Fewer than 1% were ever appealed.

Here's the part almost nobody uses: after your insurer's final
denial, you can demand an external review by an independent
reviewer they don't employ and can't pay. By federal law, they
have to accept that reviewer's decision.

You have 4 months to file. 45 days for a decision.
72 hours if it's urgent.

One letter. Most people never send it.

Would you appeal, or just pay it? 👇

#MedicalBills #InsuranceDenied #KnowYourRights

I was told my appeal was denied due to the incorrect word placing on the paperwork. Instead of “refill” the word “replacement” was needed to indicated to have my damaged medication to be replaced. 

I am almost 3 months behind on my treatment for my tumor. 

Accredo Specialty Pharmacy has yet to help or reach out in this matter.

Aetna did NOT reach out to me to inform me or my doctors of the results of the appeal.

I have spent $1,400 on temporary nerve blocks to get me through the severe debilitating pain I experience EVERYDAY!

Texas Department of State Health Services needs to be aware of how this is being handled.

Our Community needs to be aware of how Aetna allowed VERBIAGE to dictate to the outcome of VITAL medication their patient is needing!!

KHOU 11 News ABC13 Houston

Gave us wrong fax number to send in Texas Department of Insurance Independent Review. Anyone know a good lawyer to sue Aetna? They are about to cause my wife permanent, irreversible damage.

Aetna screws us over again! Aetna decided to cut funding 8/30 - just found out today talk about giving a family some warning. Soooooooooooooooo............

I have a sales post up in ELA! One is nothing over 25 the other nothing over 12.

Please take a look! If you see anything you like please claim or send me an offer cause EVERYTHING has to go.  

I also have a go fund me up:
https://gofund.me/a70b0cf6a

If you can donate great if not absolutely fine all I ask is that you share it out and spread the word.

Thank you! 
Kendra

Aetna/Guardian
We went out of Network with Aetna 1/1/2026. I just received an EOB showing us as In Network. I notice that they are using the Guardian fee schedule which we are in network with. Is this something that we can contest since we didn’t receive a notification from Aetna or Guardian?

I also noticed this is happening with Cigna as well. We have been in practice 20 years and Dr started out contracted with every possible insurance you can be with. We are losing money on certain procedures and I want to go out of Network with everything. Dr wants to go out of network with one plan once a year. That was working until they started putting us back in network with other plans. Any advice? Thank you for your time and help it’s greatly appreciated

Update to my old post from months ago…  yesterday I FINALLY got a health insurance waiver APPROVED for my son’s college!!  This means the $6,000 annual charge will be removed from my bill!!  I’m SO relieved!!  It took me seven lengthy phone calls to Aetna (our health insurance) since we have an HMO and every time I called I got a different answer.  Thanks to all the people here who encouraged me to ask for “reciprocity agreements” as that was the key phrase!  I kept running into road blocks and my request to get a waiver was denied 5 times!  I kept appealing again.   Finally found out I needed a new primary care doctor for my college son in Oregon (we are from California) and after he selected someone and a new medical group in the Portland area then we got a letter proving that, submitted that to appeal AGAIN and it WORKED!!  They approved it!!

Since I am on a 10 payment plan for the school year my July and August payments were $600 higher than they should have been because of the health insurance charge.  ($6,000 per year / 10 payments = $600 extra on each payment.)

So today I call the business office at the school and that $1200 will be counted towards a credit on my balance.  Making the remaining 8 payments even lower!

And my son who didn’t receive a Pell grant I asked them why?  I thought our income qualified with 4 kids (family of six, this kid going to college is oldest).  They looked into it, then said he qualified for $3,869 in a Pell Grant!

So my payments will go down even more!  I’m saying my prayers of gratitude tonight!!!  🙏🙏🙏

Also, want to say thank you to ALL the people here who tried to offer me helpful suggestions to get this health insurance appeal!!  💕

If I had just accepted the “no” I kept getting it would have cost us an extra $6k PER year.  $24k+ over 4 years!  Maybe more if fees went up!!

I’m SO RELIEVED to not have to pay that now!  🥰

By the way, at least 5 different call center customer service people flat out told me an HMO in California would NEVER cover in Oregon.  They were all wrong.  It does with a “reciprocity agreement” and changing your medical group and PCP.
